title: Experimental test of the intrinsic dimensionality of Hounsfield unit measurements
author: Zachary Levine
license_note: Confirmed via CrossRef DOI metadata: dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.sw3efgn
materials: 1. Medical CT scan of 30 elemental powders:
4. Comparison of experimental and theoretical results

steps.title: Prepare sample bottles
steps.instruction: Place 33 samples in nominally identical 15 mL polyethylene bottles: 31 powders representing the first 20 chemical elements, one water sample, and one empty bottle (air) for volume determination.

steps.title: Weigh each sample
steps.instruction: Weigh each bottle before and after adding the powder or water to obtain the mass of each powder and the water.

steps.title: Arrange bottles on imaging platform
steps.instruction: Place the bottles on a low‑density but rigid foam platform ready for CT scanning.

steps.title: Acquire CT scans at four kV
steps.instruction: Using a Siemens SOMATOM CT (Veterans’ Administration Hospital, Baltimore, MD, USA), perform axial scans with the Syngo CT 2012B chest routine protocol at tube voltages 80 kV, 100 kV, 120 kV, and 140 kV. Keep all other parameters identical: voxel size 0.3125 mm × 0.3125 mm × 0.625 mm, integrated tube current 100 mAs, same reconstruction algorithm and field of view.

steps.title: Identify bottle boundaries in images
steps.instruction: Visually inspect each image stack to locate the first and last slices that contain each plastic bottle.

steps.title: Segment empty bottle
steps.instruction: For the empty bottle, apply a threshold of –800 HU to separate bottle material from air; treat pixels > –350 HU as the supporting platform. Test thresholds from –810 HU to –790 HU and note that average bottle intensity varies only 2‑3 % across this range at all kV levels.

steps.title: Process empty‑bottle clusters
steps.instruction: Collect clusters of pixels > –800 HU, erode to remove isolated noisy pixels, fill small holes, and select the largest cluster as the empty bottle. Count its pixels to determine bottle volume and compute the average pixel intensity of those voxels.

steps.title: Process sample bottles
steps.instruction: Segment each non‑empty bottle in the same way, then subtract (a) the pixel count corresponding to the empty‑bottle volume and (b) the integrated pixel intensities representing the plastic bottle (obtained from the empty‑bottle measurement) to obtain corrected HU values for the sample material.

steps.title: Construct experimental HU‑per‑molar matrix
steps.instruction: For the 30 measured samples at each of the four tube voltages, compute Hounsfield units per (mole · m⁻³) to form matrix H. Assemble composition matrix C containing the number of atoms of the 13 elements in each sample. Solve for matrix A by minimizing the residual |C A – H|².

steps.title: Generate theoretical HU‑per‑molar matrix
steps.instruction: Obtain XCOM photon cross‑section data, combine with a tungsten anode spectral model using interpolating cubic splines (TASMICS), apply a one‑parameter filter and a simple detector model, and compute theoretical HU per (mole · m⁻³) for the first 20 chemical elements, forming a matrix analogous to the experimental one.

steps.title: Fit theoretical curves
steps.instruction: Fit the theoretical curves using a single filter‑thickness parameter and determine its 95 % confidence interval.

steps.title: Apply SVD and BIC analysis
steps.instruction: Perform Singular Value Decomposition on both the experimental and theoretical molar‑potency matrices and use the Bayesian Information Criterion to decide the number of significant singular values.
